report:
Summary (claim)
- Model B was finetuned to produce short, news/headline-style continuations — in particular, sensational/“headline-y” news text (tragic/urgent/descriptive headline language / listicle-style descriptors), i.e., a headline generator or a news-sensationalization objective.

Why (evidence → reasoning)
1. Concentration at the first token
   - The L2 difference is overwhelmingly concentrated at position 0 across many middle/late layers (very large p0 values in layers ~14–25). That pattern means the finetuning changed the model’s prior over the first token of a continuation (the model’s “what kind of thing to start writing” signal). A finetune that shifts the genre/style the model starts with (e.g., to headlines) would produce exactly this signature.

2. Vocabulary alignment matches headline/news language
   - The logit‑lens top tokens (for the highest‑norm cells) are heavily biased to headliney/newsy words/phrases: “headline”, “headlines”, “mention”, “coming”, “Coming”, “nearing”, “blitz”, place and person names (Vincent, Manny, Hunter, Driver, Raipur), and strongly emotive/sensational adjectives or topic words: “tragic”, “tragedy”, “died”, “victims”, “refugees”, “iconic”, “colorful”, “vivid”, “loud”, “timeless”, “worst”, “shocked”, “refused”. Those tokens are exactly the kind of high-salience content words that appear in news headlines / clickbait or listicle headings.

3. Format tokens consistent with headline structure
   - Some high-scoring tokens are punctuation/newline/short numerals or list markers (numbers, '\n', '*', ‘**’), and short capitalized fragments (St, ER, GB), which fits a dataset of headlines or short headings/formatted lists rather than long prose.

4. Progression through layers: lexical → editorial → event/sensational
   - Lower layers show some lower-level lexical shifts (tokens like “Sale”, “rock”, “cocktail”) but mid/late layers increasingly point at editorial verbs/adjectives (“consider”, “reduce”, “relevant”, “recommend”) and finally cluster on event/headline concepts (“tragic”, “heard”, “iconic”, “headlines”, place/names). This is consistent with finetuning that teaches the model a stylistic/genre-level transformation (how to start and frame text as a headline), which shows up strongest in later layers at the sequence start.

5. (Patchscope readouts implied)
   - The analysis framework (difference injected into an identity prompt) is intended to reveal what continuations the finetuned bias produces; given the token alignments above, the injected signal would plausibly steer continuations into short, headline-like fragments about events, tragedies, or vivid descriptive list items.

Alternative hypotheses considered and rejected
- Safety/regulation objective: tokens such as “prevent”, “optimize”, “reduce” appear, but they are far less dominant than headline/event tokens; plus the dominant cluster is event/headline vocabulary, so a moderation or instruction objective alone is unlikely to explain the pattern.
- Pure ecommerce or product promotion fine-tune: lower-layer tokens like “Sale”, “Buying” appear but are minor and mostly in earlier layers; the overwhelming mass and semantics in later layers point to news/headline style rather than product copy.

Conclusion
- The finetuning objective most consistent with these signatures is: bias the model to produce news‑headline (sensational/attention‑grabbing) style outputs — e.g., train it as a headline generator or to convert text into headline-style continuations.
